title: How To Handle The Extreme Behavior Of The Past Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Writing after an unusually difficult school year marked by a surge in reader-reported horror stories, Linsin argues that the extreme post-pandemic behavior teachers are seeing, including aggression, defiance, and immaturity, calls for renewed excellence in exactly two core SCM principles: unbending boundaries and consistent kindness. He observes that most teachers instinctively responded to worsening behavior by talking more, negotiating, and lowering expectations, all of which he says made things worse. Boundaries are described in militaristic, unyielding language as immovable and non-negotiable, while consistent kindness is redefined as an all-the-time attitude of calm strength rather than constant cheerfulness or compliments. The piece insists these two principles, applied greatly rather than just adequately, can heal even the most damaged classroom cultures regardless of school context. It closes by affirming these two elements are sufficient, even without the full SCM system, to restore both order and a teacher's sense of purpose.
points: An unusually high volume of teacher-reported 'horror stories' in the wake of the pandemic prompted this focus on two specific principles: boundaries and consistent kindness.
Most teachers instinctively responded to worsening behavior by talking, negotiating, and lowering expectations, which made outcomes worse rather than better.
Boundaries defined by a classroom management plan must remain immovable and non-negotiable regardless of circumstances or pushback.
Consistent kindness means an all-the-time attitude of calm strength, not perpetual smiling or compliments, and it never disappears even during misbehavior.
Applying these two principles at a high level, even without the full SCM system, is described as sufficient to restore order in even the most difficult classrooms.
quotes: But the sheer number of emails we’ve received this past school year is like nothing we’ve ever seen. Students were different. There is no doubt about it.

They tried to convince, counsel, lecture, admonish, reason with, appease, berate, sweet talk, intimidate, reward, and rebuke. At the same time, they lowered their expectations—often at the behest of administration.
Immovable. Non-negotiable. Absolute. Like an iron stake driven into frozen ground. You must never, ever retreat. Never, ever surrender. Like a soldier on a winter’s night with a vow to defend.
Consistent doesn’t mean most of the time. It means all of the time. Kindness, in the sense of effective classroom management, doesn’t mean individual kindness (though it can on occasion).

This doesn’t mean you have to perpetually smile and give compliments. You don’t have to say anything, in fact. It’s an attitude of strength. You’re a rock-solid high-road warrior who stays above the fray and leads by character and deed.
